messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Señor García is a 67-year-old widowed prosecutor who has been struggling with the aftermath of a sexual assault that occurred two years ago. The event left him profoundly shaken and has significantly impacted his daily life. Señor García’s trauma began when he was assaulted in a public park late at night by someone known to him, an acquaintance from work. This intimate violation made being around familiar faces particularly triggering for him, especially if children were present, as it reminded him of the vulnerability associated with such situations. Señor García vividly recalls every detail of the assault—the cold chill that settled on his skin, the fear and helplessness he felt, and how acutely aware he was of every sound and movement around him. This vividness is so intense that the memory feels present rather than past, as though it continues to unfold right now. For instance, when Señor García sees children playing in a park or any known person from his work, these scenes instantly transport him back to that night, making the assault feel current and immediate. The memory’s uncontrolled access has made life increasingly difficult for Señor García. He avoids going to unfamiliar places because he cannot assess potential dangers adequately. This avoidance is compounded by his constant scanning of exits whenever he enters any room or building. The mere presence of a specific temperature on his skin, reminiscent of that cold night, triggers these vivid memories and intensifies his sense of vulnerability. What frightens Señor García most are the thoughts that his body has been permanently damaged by what happened, and he feels dirty or contaminated as a result. This contamination belief is so pervasive that it influences how he interacts with others and perceives the world around him. He believes that the world is inherently dangerous, and this belief exacerbates his sense of threat. For instance, while at work prosecuting cases, Señor García constantly scans for potential weapons or any objects that could pose a risk, reinforcing his conviction that the environment is not safe. The contamination he feels also leads to an obsessive avoidance of certain people and places. He finds it increasingly challenging to attend social gatherings or even go to familiar locales where he might encounter known individuals or see children playing. These triggers fuel his vivid memories, which in turn exacerbate his negative appraisals about the world being dangerous and himself being permanently damaged. Señor García’s avoidance behaviors have had significant consequences. His work as a prosecutor has become particularly arduous because of the constant threat he perceives, leading to missed court dates and increased stress at his job. Additionally, his social life has diminished significantly; he avoids gatherings with friends and family out of fear that these settings might trigger intrusive memories or negative appraisals. Despite his efforts to manage his symptoms, Señor García's condition has worsened over time. The tight loop of triggers, vivid memories, negative appraisals, and heightened threat perception has created a self-reinforcing cycle where each element amplifies the others. He finally decided to seek help because he was struggling with basic tasks at work and in his daily life, realizing that his symptoms were interfering too much with his ability to function effectively. Señor García hopes that through therapy, he can regain control over his memories and reduce his sense of contamination and vulnerability. His primary fear is being unable to protect himself from further harm or experiencing another traumatic event, which underscores the urgency in seeking professional help.
